2-1.question: Which of these are valid Sequences (Chow)? Select all that apply.
2-1.explanation: A Chow is 3 consecutive tiles in one suit, so {{s8}}{{s9}}{{s1}} fails because sequences do not wrap around and {{m6}}{{p7}}{{s8}} mixes three suits.

2-1.question: Match each three-tile group to what it is.
2-1.explanation: Consecutive same-suit tiles make a Chow; a gap breaks the run, 9-1-2 wraps around the end, and honor tiles have no numbers at all.

2-1.question: How many tiles are in one Sequence (Chow)?
2-1.explanation: A Chow is exactly 3 consecutive tiles, which is why four Chows plus a pair fill the 14-tile winning hand.

2-1.question: Select the middle tile that completes this Sequence: {{m4}}___{{m6}}
2-1.explanation: {{m4}}{{m5}}{{m6}} is the only run through both given tiles, so {{m5}} is the one tile that fits in the gap.

2-1.question: Arrange these tiles into the highest possible valid Sequence.
2-1.explanation: 7-8-9 is the highest Chow in any suit, because 8-9-1 would wrap around and is never allowed.

2-2.question: Which of these are valid Pongs (Triplets)? Select all that apply.
2-2.explanation: A Pong is 3 identical tiles of any type, so the three Wests and three 9-Bamboo both count, while {{m2}}{{m3}}{{m4}} is a Chow and the three different Dragons are not identical.

2-2.question: Select the tile that makes a Pong out of your pair, not a Chow: {{p7}}{{p7}}___
2-2.explanation: A Pong needs 3 identical tiles, so the pair needs a third {{p7}}; {{p6}} or {{p8}} would not complete any meld.

2-2.question: How many identical tiles are needed to make a Pong?
2-2.explanation: A Pong is exactly 3 identical tiles, while a 4th copy of the same tile would make it a Kong instead.

2-2.question: Match each Pong term to its meaning.
2-2.explanation: A Pong is 3 identical tiles, and it is concealed when you drew all three yourself but exposed when the third came from another player's discard.

2-2.question: Why is {{east}}{{east}}{{east}} a valid Pong but {{east}}{{south}}{{west}} is not?
options: Honor tiles have no numbers, so only identical copies can form a meld
Winds may only be used in pairs
2-2.explanation: Winds and Dragons carry no rank, so they can never line up as consecutive tiles and only identical copies can form a Pong.

2-3.question: Match each hand part to how many tiles it uses.
2-3.explanation: The pair is the only 2-tile unit; Chow and Pong both use 3 tiles and a Kong uses 4, yet each meld still counts as 3 for hand structure.

2-3.question: Select the tile that completes this pair: {{p3}}___
2-3.explanation: A pair is 2 identical tiles, so {{p3}}{{p3}} is the pair; {{p2}} or {{p4}} would only start a run.

2-3.question: Which of these can serve as the pair (eyes) of a winning hand? Select all that apply.
2-3.explanation: Any two identical tiles can be the eyes, so a West pair and a Red Dragon pair both work, but {{m3}}{{m4}} and {{east}}{{south}} are not identical.

2-3.question: Which statement about the pair is correct?
options: A hand may hold two pairs if it has only three melds
A hand with 4 melds and 2 pairs is a valid win
A standard win is 4 melds plus exactly 1 pair
The pair must always be a suited tile
2-3.explanation: The standard hand is 4 melds + exactly 1 pair = 14 tiles, so an extra pair leaves the hand one meld short.

2-3.question: How many tiles are in a Pair (eyes)?
2-3.explanation: A pair is 2 identical tiles, and a winning hand contains exactly one such pair.

2-4.question: Which of these are Kongs? Select all that apply.
2-4.explanation: A Kong is 4 identical tiles of any type, so four 7-Bamboo and four Red Dragons qualify, while three 1-Character is a Pong and {{p4}}{{p5}}{{p6}} is a Chow.

2-4.question: Match each Kong type to how it is formed.

pairs.right: 4th tile added to an existing Pong

2-4.explanation: The three Kongs differ only in where the 4th tile comes from: your own draws, another player's discard, or upgrading a Pong you already exposed.

2-4.question: How many Kongs does the 十八羅漢 (18 Arhats) hand require?
2-4.explanation: 十八羅漢 is the four-Kong limit hand: 4 Kongs of 4 tiles each plus a pair makes 18 physical tiles.

2-4.question: Select the tile that upgrades this Pong into a Kong: {{m7}}{{m7}}{{m7}}___
2-4.explanation: A Kong is 4 identical tiles, so adding the last {{m7}} turns the Pong into a supplemental Kong.

2-4.question: A Kong is 4 tiles, so why does a hand with one Kong still count as a normal 4-meld hand?
options: Because the Kong replaces your pair
Because a Kong counts as one 3-tile meld and the replacement draw restores your hand size
Because Kongs are ignored when scoring structure
Because you discard one tile after declaring a Kong
2-4.explanation: A Kong counts as a single meld (3 tiles) for structure, and the replacement draw keeps your hand at the right size, so the hand is still 4 melds + 1 pair.

2-5.question: Which of these are valid winning-hand structures? Select all that apply.
2-5.explanation: Any mix of 4 melds plus 1 pair wins, but 4 Pongs + 1 Kong is 5 melds with no pair and 3 Pongs + 1 Pair is only 11 tiles.

2-5.question: You hold {{m1}}{{m2}}{{m3}} {{p4}}{{p5}}{{p6}} {{s7}}{{s8}}{{s9}} {{east}}{{east}}{{east}} {{m9}}. Select the tile that completes the win.
2-5.explanation: The hand already has 4 melds, so the 13th tile only needs to pair up: {{m9}}{{m9}} is the eyes and completes 14 tiles.

2-5.question: Match each structure term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The one pair a hand needs
4 identical tiles counted as one meld

2-5.explanation: Every winning hand is 4 melds of these three kinds plus the single pair known as the eyes.

2-5.question: A hand of four Kongs plus a pair physically shows how many tiles?
2-5.explanation: Each Kong adds one extra physical tile to the 14-tile frame, so 4 Kongs + 1 pair shows 18 tiles.

2-5.question: Rank matters in a Chow: arrange these Character tiles from lowest to highest.
2-5.explanation: Character tiles run 1 to 9, so the ascending order is {{m2}}{{m5}}{{m8}} — the same reading order a Chow must follow.

2-6.question: Match each combination to its tile count.
2-6.explanation: The four building blocks are 2, 3, 3 and 4 tiles, and only the Kong's extra tile is absorbed by a replacement draw.

2-6.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: A Chow must stay within one suit
A Kong counts as one meld for hand structure
A pair of Dragons adds 1 Faan
Honor tiles can form a Chow
2-6.explanation: Chows never mix suits and a Kong is one meld, but a Dragon pair adds no Faan and honors cannot form runs at all.

2-6.question: You hold {{s2}}{{s3}}{{s4}} {{p6}}{{p7}}{{p8}} {{m5}}{{m5}}{{m5}} {{west}}{{west}}{{west}} {{red}}. Select the tile that completes 4 melds + 1 pair.
2-6.explanation: With four melds already set, the lone {{red}} only needs a partner, so a second Red Dragon completes the eyes.

2-6.question: Which of these is NOT a valid winning hand?
2-6.explanation: The third option is only 3 melds and two pairs, which is 13 tiles with the wrong shape, while the others are all 4 melds + 1 pair.

2-6.question: How many Faan are needed to declare a win in Hong Kong mahjong?
2-6.explanation: Three Faan is the minimum to win (三番起糊), and 10 Faan is the cap on any hand.
